response.task_summary: Predict whether a household/person is likely to receive food stamp/SNAP benefits using socioeconomic signals that should generalize across geographic and temporal shifts.

ranking.rationale: Number of workers in the family is a direct, stable proxy for household earned-income capacity and SNAP need.
Weeks worked strongly captures annual labor-force attachment, a robust determinant of low-income program eligibility.
Usual weekly hours worked is a core measure of employment intensity and likely household resources.
Whether the person worked last week is a salient indicator of current employment and financial strain.
Educational attainment is a broadly stable predictor of earnings potential and poverty risk across domains.
Presence and ages of children strongly affect household needs and SNAP participation incentives.
Age is broadly predictive through life-cycle effects on work, dependency, and eligibility-related household composition.
Marital status helps capture household structure and economic support patterns relevant to food assistance.
Relationship to household reference person informs family role and dependency structure tied to benefit receipt.
Disability status is a meaningful, semantically stable correlate of reduced earnings and higher assistance need.
Looking for work indicates unemployment-related hardship that should generalize across settings.
Layoff status is a direct signal of recent labor-market disruption and likely temporary need.
Public coverage often co-occurs with low income, though it risks some policy-environment dependence.
Recent childbirth can materially increase household expenses and temporarily reduce labor supply.
Cognitive difficulty can affect employability and need, though partly overlaps with broader disability measures.
Hearing difficulty may modestly predict labor-market barriers and assistance need.
Vision difficulty similarly captures functional limitation but is less central than core work variables.
Occupation can reflect earnings and job stability, but detailed codes may be brittle across domains.
Sex may correlate with labor-force patterns and caregiving, but it is also a demographic shortcut to downweight.
Military service may weakly relate to benefits and employment history but is not central for SNAP prediction.
English ability can affect labor-market access, yet it also risks encoding immigrant-status shortcuts.
Nativity may correlate with eligibility and income but is largely demographic and potentially non-robust.
Citizenship status affects formal eligibility but can act as a brittle policy-linked shortcut across domains.
Race may capture structural inequities but is a sensitive demographic shortcut with poor OOD semantics.
Place of birth is mostly demographic and likely to encode subgroup or regional artifacts rather than stable need.
Ancestry is weakly connected to SNAP need and mainly serves as a demographic proxy.
Survey year can capture temporal shifts and policy changes but is a domain identifier rather than a causal predictor.
State is the clearest domain identifier and likely to induce spurious geographic shortcuts under distribution shift.
